section.title: Bless the Lord, O My Soul
section.sectionRationale: David's mature, sweeping hymn of pure gratitude moves from a soul stirred to remember God's kind deeds, forgiveness, healing, and compassion, out to God's covenant faithfulness across generations, and finally to the whole cosmos summoned to bless the LORD, its themes of steadfast love and complete forgiveness fulfilled in Christ.
section.thesis: Because the LORD forgives all iniquity, heals every disease, and shows compassion as high as the heavens and as far as the east is from the west, the whole soul, and indeed all creation, is summoned to bless His holy name and never forget His kind deeds.
section.frameNote: Four movements: a personal call to bless the LORD and remember His benefits, verses 1-5; God's righteous, compassionate character revealed to Moses and Israel, verses 6-14; human frailty set against the LORD's everlasting steadfast love, verses 15-19; and a cosmic chorus of angels, hosts, and all creation blessing the LORD, verses 20-22.

units.label: Do not forget all His kind deeds
units.note: a personal call to remember God's benefits

verses.text: Of David. {{barak|Bless}} the LORD, O my soul; all that is within me, bless His holy name.
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds,
He who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases,
who redeems your life from the Pit and crowns you with loving devotion and compassion,
who satisfies you with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's.

units.label: The Lord is compassionate and gracious
units.note: God's righteous character revealed to Moses and Israel

verses.text: The LORD executes righteousness and justice for all the oppressed.
He made known His ways to Moses, His deeds to the people of Israel.
The LORD is {{rachum|compassionate}} and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in {{chesed|loving devotion}}.
He will not always accuse us, nor harbor His anger forever.
He has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our iniquities.
For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is His loving devotion for those who fear Him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us.
As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him.
For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust.

units.label: His loving devotion extends to those who fear Him
units.note: human frailty against God's everlasting love

verses.text: As for man, his days are like grass, he blooms like a flower of the field;
when the wind passes over, it vanishes, and its place remembers it no more.
But from everlasting to everlasting the loving devotion of the LORD extends to those who fear Him, and His righteousness to their children's children,
to those who keep His covenant and remember to obey His precepts.
The LORD has established His throne in heaven, and His kingdom rules over all.

units.label: Bless the Lord, all His works
units.note: a cosmic chorus of angels, hosts, and all creation

verses.text: Bless the LORD, all His angels mighty in strength who carry out His word, who hearken to the voice of His command.
Bless the LORD, all His hosts, you servants who do His will.
Bless the LORD, all His works in all places of His dominion. Bless the LORD, O my soul!

barak.gloss: To bless, kneel in adoring gratitude. David commands his own soul to this posture, more than polite thanks, a deliberate, whole-being act of worship that frames the entire psalm from its first word to its last.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant love. Repeated across this psalm as the ground of forgiveness, compassion, and everlasting faithfulness, this is the same love fully revealed and secured for sinners at the cross.

rachum.gloss: Compassionate, deeply and tenderly merciful. Paired with 'gracious' and 'slow to anger,' this echoes God's own self-revelation to Moses in Exodus 34:6, the classic Old Testament description of His character.

basic.context: In this mature, gratitude-filled hymn, David commands his own soul to bless the LORD and never forget His kind deeds, forgiveness, healing, redemption, and compassion. The psalm sweeps from personal benefits, to God's covenant character revealed to Moses, to the fleeting brevity of human life set against God's everlasting love, and finally to a summons for angels, hosts, and all creation to bless the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: Unlike many of David's psalms, this one names no enemy and no crisis, its focus is pure remembrance and gratitude, showing that worship need not wait for deliverance from trouble but can flow simply from rehearsing what God has already done and who He already is.
basic.originalLanguages: David commands his soul to barak, bless, the LORD, a deliberate posture of adoring gratitude. God is described as rachum, compassionate, and abounding in chesed, loving devotion, the very words God used to describe Himself to Moses, Exodus 34:6, and to which this whole psalm returns again and again.
basic.typology: Every benefit David lists, forgiveness, healing, redemption from the Pit, crowning with loving devotion, is embodied fully in Christ, who forgave sins, healed diseases, and redeemed lives from the pit of death through His own cross and resurrection, while the fatherly compassion of verse 13 anticipates the father's compassion in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son, Luke 15:20.
basic.christ: Jesus embodies every benefit this psalm names: He forgave sins, Mark 2:5, healed every kind of disease, Matthew 4:23, and redeemed His people from the pit of death through the cross, Colossians 1:13-14. The psalm's picture of fatherly compassion, verse 13, is the very compassion the father shows the returning son in Luke 15:20, and the everlasting throne of verse 19 belongs, in the New Testament, to Christ Himself, Hebrews 1:8.
basic.god: God is the one who forgives all iniquity and heals all disease, executes righteousness for the oppressed, and is compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, removing sin as far as the east is from the west and extending His faithfulness from everlasting to everlasting to those who fear Him.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 34:6-7 supplies the classic self-revelation of God's character that this psalm echoes throughout, compassionate, gracious, slow to anger. Micah 7:18-19 likewise pictures sin cast into the depths of the sea. Isaiah 40:6-8 compares human life to grass, quoted again in 1 Peter 1:24-25. Luke 15:20 shows the father's compassion embodied in Jesus' own parable of grace.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's sweeping call for the whole soul, and indeed all creation, to bless the LORD for His forgiveness, healing, redemption, and everlasting steadfast love finds its full answer in Christ, in whom every one of these kind deeds is accomplished for sinners once and for all.

context.literary:
The psalm has twenty two verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, though it is not an acrostic; the length gives it the feel of something complete, a whole alphabet of praise. It moves in widening rings. Verses 1 to 5 are a private address, 'you' and 'your,' as the singular voice talks to its own soul. Verses 6 to 18 switch to 'us' and 'our': the people, and then 'those who fear Him.' Verses 19 to 22 open to the whole realm, angels, hosts and every work of God in every place. Then the last line collapses the circle back to where it began, 'Bless the LORD, O my soul!' The first and last lines are a frame, and everything between has been the soul's schooling.

Within the first ring the benefits come as a list of five participles, forgiving, healing, redeeming, crowning, satisfying. Notice the order. Forgiveness comes first and is paired with healing; the pit comes next; and only then the crown and the good things. The man is rescued from the worst before he is honoured.

The middle section is built on comparisons that get closer to home. The love of God is as high as the heavens are above the earth (verse 11), then as far as east from west (verse 12), then as near as a father's compassion (verse 13). Each simile shrinks in scale, from the sky, to the horizon, to a household. Verse 14 is the hinge: 'He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust.' After it comes the contrast with grass (verses 15 and 16) and a second 'But' that lifts the eye back to God (verse 17).

Three phrases recur like a refrain. 'Loving devotion' appears in verses 4, 8, 11 and 17; 'those who fear Him' in verses 11, 13 and 17; and 'bless' opens each of the five calls that frame the psalm, verses 1, 2, 20, 21 and 22.
context.historical:
The heading gives the psalm to David, and the shape of the thinking fits a king who has been forgiven much and rescued often. Some scholars have noticed Aramaic coloured forms in the Hebrew and suspect a later hand, but nothing in the text forces a date, and the church has mostly kept the heading. What is certain is that the psalm is rooted in a very early moment in Israel's life, the revelation at Sinai.

Verse 7 says, 'He made known His ways to Moses, His deeds to the people of Israel.' That points straight to Exodus 33 and 34. After the golden calf, Moses begged, 'let me know Your ways' (Exodus 33:13), and the LORD answered by passing before him and proclaiming His name, 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion' (Exodus 34:6). The people had been told 'stiff-necked' and nearly consumed (Exodus 32:9-10), yet the LORD relented (Exodus 32:14). Psalm 103 is a long meditation on what Israel learned that day: the God who knew they were idolaters chose to forgive. Verses 8 to 10 are almost a quotation of Exodus 34, with one telling omission. The warning that He will 'by no means leave the guilty unpunished' is not repeated; the psalm dwells on the side of the name that has become the people's hope.

Verse 12's picture of sin removed to the far horizon would have been heard against the Day of Atonement, when the high priest confessed Israel's iniquities over a live goat that carried them 'into a solitary place' (Leviticus 16:21-22). The audience knew what it looked like to have sin sent away.

The eagle in verse 5 is the image Israelite poets use for strength regained. Deuteronomy 32:11 pictures God carrying His people as an eagle carries its young, and Isaiah 40:31 promises that those who wait on the LORD 'will mount up with wings like eagles.' The sense of verse 5 is that the one who has been forgiven and delivered finds the vigour of youth return. Verse 5's first line is among the harder phrases in the Hebrew, and translations differ on what exactly God satisfies, but the renewed youth is clear.
context.canonical:
The words of verse 8 are the most repeated description of God in the Old Testament. They begin at Exodus 34:6 and return in Numbers 14:18 (as Moses pleads for a rebellious people), Nehemiah 9:17, Psalm 86:15, Psalm 145:8, Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2. In Jonah the formula is a complaint: the prophet knew God was 'gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion,' and so ran. Psalm 103 is the one place where the formula is turned into a full hymn rather than a plea or a protest.

The psalm belongs with its neighbours. Psalm 102 had cried, 'my days are like lengthening shadows, and I wither away like grass'; Psalm 103 replies, 'As for man, his days are like grass,' and then sets the permanence of God beside it. Psalm 104 begins and ends with the identical call, 'Bless the LORD, O my soul,' and moves from redemption to creation. The pair, one about salvation and the other about the world God made, belong together in Israel's praise.

The New Testament absorbs the psalm quietly. Mary's Magnificat takes verse 17: 'His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation' (Luke 1:50). Jesus' healings and forgiveness of the paralytic (Mark 2:5-12) enact verse 3 in person, and Matthew 8:16-17 explains the healings through Isaiah 53. Paul's 'blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven' (Romans 4:7-8), quoting Psalm 32, belongs to the same family of thought. The father in Luke 15:20 who 'was filled with compassion' and ran to his son is verse 13 turned into a story. And the great chorus of Revelation 5:11-13 and 7:11-12, with angels and 'every creature' blessing God, fulfils verses 20 to 22 in the fullest scale.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted hearers to learn how to talk to themselves. The opening command, 'Bless the LORD, O my soul,' treats the inner life as something to be preached to, because it forgets. Verse 2 gives the reason: 'do not forget all His kind deeds.' Forgetfulness, not unbelief, is the first danger, and gratitude must be done on purpose.

He also meant them to hold onto the right picture of God when they felt the weight of their sin. Verses 8 to 14 reply to the voice that says God is waiting to punish. He is slow to anger, He has not repaid us as we deserved, He has removed our transgressions beyond reach. A listener who had known the sting of exile or personal guilt would hear this as permission to hope.

Finally, he wanted the praise to widen. A song that began with 'my soul' ends by recruiting angels, armies and every work of God. The psalm teaches that private gratitude is a rehearsal for a chorus that already exists. The one who sings is joining something larger than himself, and the reasons for singing have been given to a whole people, to Moses and to 'those who fear Him' across the generations.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The list of benefits in verses 3 to 5 is the psalmist's own testimony: God has forgiven, healed and redeemed him. It describes what David knew of the LORD. It is not a contract that guarantees every believer a cure for every sickness, and Scripture itself shows faithful people who prayed and were not healed, such as Paul's thorn in 2 Corinthians 12:7-9. The verse proclaims God's character and power; it does not set a formula for the time or manner.

The statement that He has 'not dealt with us according to our sins' (verse 10) describes the pattern of grace, not a licence. The next verses tie it to those who fear Him, and verse 18 speaks of those who 'keep His covenant and remember to obey His precepts.' Grace is the ground of obedience, not a substitute for it. The imperatives, on the other hand, are plain commands: bless the LORD, do not forget, and (to angels and creation) bless Him. Those are meant to be done, today, by any reader. The Father's fatherly compassion in verse 13 is also not a loose picture of divine softness; it is attached to those who fear Him, and it is how the New Testament describes the relationship of believers to God, Romans 8:15.

debates.question: Does 'heals all your diseases' (verse 3) promise physical healing?

views.label: Yes, in this life, as an ordinary benefit of redemption
views.case: The verb is the ordinary verb for physical healing and is set beside forgiveness. Some Christians read Isaiah 53:5, 'by His stripes we are healed,' with Matthew 8:17 as grounds for expecting bodily healing as part of what Christ bought. On that reading verse 3 invites bold prayer for healing now.

views.label: The healing is mostly spiritual, a poetic restatement of forgiveness
views.case: Hebrew poetry often says one thing twice. Forgiveness of iniquity and healing of disease are parallel lines, and 'disease' often stands for the wound of sin, as in Isaiah 53 and Psalm 41:4. 1 Peter 2:24 uses 'by His stripes you are healed' in the context of dying to sin and living to righteousness.

views.label: Real healing of body and soul, with the full cure reserved for the resurrection
views.case: The psalm does not narrow the verse either way. God does heal, and the New Testament shows Jesus healing all who came to Him. Yet Romans 8:11 places the final restoration of the mortal body in the resurrection, and Revelation 21:4 promises the end of pain, so that every present healing is a down payment.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is preferred, the verse tells the sufferer who the Healer is and sets healing inside the whole of God's kindness. It cannot be used to say that the sick lack faith, because the psalm itself later reminds us that we are dust.

debates.question: How do verses 10 to 12 fit with the demand that those who receive mercy must also 'keep His covenant' (verse 18)?

views.label: Forgiveness is unconditional, obedience is its fruit
views.case: Verses 10 to 12 describe what God has done without any mention of what we do. Verse 18 then describes those who in fact live in that grace: they keep covenant and remember His precepts. The reformers read it this way, with obedience as the response of the forgiven rather than the price of forgiveness.

views.label: The covenant blessing is conditioned on faithfulness
views.case: Verses 11, 13 and 17 each limit the blessing to 'those who fear Him,' and verse 18 adds that they must keep the covenant. Read with Exodus 34:7, which says the guilty are not left unpunished, the psalm shows that mercy and responsibility belong together. Persistent rebellion shuts a person out of the benefits.

views.label: Both are true at once, as covenant grace always has been
views.case: Deuteronomy 7:9 says the LORD 'keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments.' Grace comes first and obedience follows, but the covenant is a real relationship in which a person can walk away.

debates.bearing: The psalm leaves the believer neither presumptuous nor anxious. Mercy is as broad as the sky, but it is received by a heart that honours the Giver.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm turns on a small family of words that English hides. In verse 2 the 'kind deeds' are gemulim, from the root gamal, which means to deal with someone, to repay, to treat. In verse 10 the same root returns in the negative: He has not 'repaid' (gamal) us according to our iniquities. So the two verses are working together. The soul is told not to forget everything God has done to it, and then we learn that what God has done is the very opposite of what was owed. The same word that could have meant payment for sin is used for the gift of forgiveness.

'Forgives' in verse 3 is salach, a verb that in the Old Testament has God alone as its subject. People may pardon an offence between themselves, using other words, but salach is the verb for the divine act of pardon, as in Numbers 14:19-20 and 1 Kings 8:30. The soul is being told to remember something only God does.

In verse 1 the soul is told to bless with 'all that is within me,' kol qerabai, literally all my inward parts, the inner organs, the seat of feeling. The psalmist is not offering a polite sentiment from the head; he wants the whole inside to join in.

Verse 8 says the LORD is 'slow to anger,' in Hebrew erekh apayim, 'long of nostrils.' Anger in Hebrew is pictured as hot breath through the nose, so a God who is 'long of nose' is one whose burning takes a long time to arrive. That is the phrase Exodus 34:6 first gave.

Verse 14 contains one of the quiet gems of the psalm. 'He knows our frame' uses yetser, from the verb yatsar, to shape as a potter shapes clay. It is the verb of Genesis 2:7, where God 'formed' the man from the dust of the ground. The psalm says that the God who formed us from the earth remembers what He used. Together with 'we are dust' (aphar, the word of Genesis 3:19), it closes the circle: He remembers our making.

Finally, verse 7 speaks of God's 'ways,' derakhim, the same word Moses used in Exodus 33:13. The ways of God, in this psalm, are not hidden policy but the character revealed in the next verse, and verse 17's 'from everlasting to everlasting' (me'olam ve'ad olam) is the exact phrase of Psalm 90:2. The God who was God before the mountains is the God whose love will outlast every grass-like human life.

typology.type: The scapegoat and sin removed 'as far as the east is from the west,' verse 12
typology.fulfillment: The goat on the Day of Atonement carried Israel's iniquities to a solitary place, Leviticus 16:21-22, and the psalm turns that into an image of distance. The correspondence in Christ is that He bears sin away through His death: 'He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, and 'to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself,' Hebrews 9:26. The animal could only show what removal looked like and had to be repeated each year; Christ's single offering secured 'eternal redemption,' Hebrews 9:12.

typology.type: The Father who has compassion, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: God as a father pitying his children is more than a figure of speech. In the parable of the lost son, the father 'was filled with compassion,' ran to the boy and clothed him, Luke 15:20-22. Jesus' own prayer begins 'Our Father,' Matthew 6:9, and Paul says believers receive 'the Spirit of sonship,' Romans 8:15. The psalm pictures a father's pity for his children; in Christ the children actually become sons and daughters by adoption. The picture remains imperfect, because no human father pities perfectly.

typology.type: The redeemed and healed life, verses 3 and 4
typology.fulfillment: Forgiveness, healing and redemption from the pit are the exact blessings the Gospels show Jesus giving. He forgives the paralytic and then heals him to show He has authority to do so, Mark 2:5-12; He heals many at evening to fulfil Isaiah 53, Matthew 8:16-17. At the cross, 'the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:5. The type is partial: bodily healing in the Gospels is a sign, and the final removal of death is still to come, Isaiah 25:8.

typology.type: The renewed youth like the eagle's, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Verse 5 sees strength restored to the one who has been forgiven. In the New Testament the renewal is resurrection life. Paul says that 'the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead' will 'give life to your mortal bodies,' Romans 8:11, and Jesus declares, 'I am the resurrection and the life,' John 11:25. Where the psalm describes a refreshing within this life, Christ promises a renewal that death cannot undo.

study.christ:
The most striking thing about this psalm is how many of its verbs the Gospels hand to Jesus. He forgives (verse 3): 'Son, your sins are forgiven,' Mark 2:5. The scribes were right about one thing, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' Mark 2:7, and the psalm shows why. Forgiveness is the one thing the Old Testament keeps for God, and when Jesus does it, He claims to be standing where God stands. He heals (verse 3) in the same story, and He redeems from the pit (verse 4), in His own words He came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, which belongs with Hebrews 9:12's 'eternal redemption.' When Luke 7:47-50 has Jesus forgive the woman who loved much, the story is Psalm 103:3 in a living room.

The psalm's theology of the cost of forgiveness is also worth tracing. Verse 10 says God does not repay us according to our sins; it does not say sin goes unanswered. Romans 3:25-26 explains how both can be true: God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice 'to demonstrate His righteousness,' so as to be 'just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.' The verb that the psalm negates, 'repaid,' is what Christ took in our place. 'The punishment that brought us peace was upon Him' (Isaiah 53:5). What Israel sang as a hope, the cross turns into a settled fact, which is why Paul can say there is redemption 'through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses,' Ephesians 1:7. When Jesus takes the cup and says it is 'poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28, the psalm's first benefit is being purchased in front of the disciples.

Verse 14 has its own pointer. God 'knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust.' Hebrews 2:14-17 says the Son shared flesh and blood and 'had to be made like His brothers in every way,' and Hebrews 4:15 adds that He is a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses. The knowledge of verse 14 is not only God's observation from above; in Christ it becomes His experience from within.

The psalm's picture of the father runs straight to the one who taught us to pray 'Our Father,' and the throne of verse 19 is, in the New Testament, shared by the Son, Hebrews 1:8.

A caution: this is not a psalm about Christ in the same sense as Psalm 22, and David is speaking of his own experience. The christological reading rests on the fact that the God who does these things is revealed more fully in Jesus, and that the New Testament shows Jesus doing them.
study.god:
The center of this psalm's doctrine of God is verse 8, which Israel received at Sinai after the golden calf. It matters that this was said after a disaster. The God who describes Himself as compassionate, gracious, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion was speaking to a people who had just broken the covenant. Mercy is not what He extends to the deserving; it is who He is toward the guilty.

Look at how thoroughly the psalm describes that mercy. It is wide: as high as the heavens (verse 11). It is far reaching: sin removed as far as east from west (verse 12). It is warm: the compassion of a father (verse 13). It is wise: He 'knows our frame' and remembers what we are made of (verse 14). And it is lasting: 'from everlasting to everlasting' (verse 17). There is no dimension in which the love of God is small.

This is not softness. Verse 6 declares that the LORD 'executes righteousness and justice for all the oppressed,' and Exodus 34:7, the verse that gives the psalm its words, adds that He will not leave the guilty unpunished. The psalm celebrates mercy because it has taken the sin seriously. Psalm 130:3-4 asks, 'If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared.' Forgiveness, in Scripture, produces fear in the good sense, awe at the God who has every right to condemn.

The psalm also shows divine knowledge that is personal. 'He knows our frame' means He is not surprised by our weakness. Psalm 78:39 says He 'remembered that they were but flesh,' and Isaiah 57:16 says He will not be angry forever because the spirit of man would grow weak. His mercy is shaped to our actual size. That sits beside a throne 'established in heaven' whose kingdom 'rules over all,' verse 19. The same God who is over everything stoops down to a single sinner.

Finally, the psalm shows a God who is worthy of every voice. Angels who obey, hosts who serve, and all His works in all places are called to bless Him. For worship, the psalm teaches that gratitude is a duty we perform against our own forgetfulness, and that the best material for praise is not our feelings but what God has revealed of Himself. We bless Him by remembering His name.

crossReferences.note: The source of verse 8's wording. After the golden calf the LORD passed before Moses and proclaimed His name. Psalm 103 keeps the part about mercy and slow anger and leaves out the clause about punishing the guilty, choosing the side of the name that Israel most needed to remember.

Moses asked, 'let me know Your ways.' Psalm 103:7 reports that God 'made known His ways to Moses.' The psalm identifies the answer: God's ways are His compassionate character, shown at the very moment Israel had most failed.

Asks who could stand if the LORD kept track of iniquities, and answers that forgiveness is with Him 'so that You may be feared.' It explains why verse 11 links great mercy with fearing God: pardon leads to reverence, not to carelessness.

Declares 'from everlasting to everlasting You are God.' Psalm 103:17 uses exactly the same phrase for God's loving devotion. The eternity of God's being and the eternity of His kindness are one thing.

Asks 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity?' and says He will 'cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea.' It is the prophetic twin of verse 12, with the sea instead of the horizon as the place where sin is lost.

All flesh is grass and the word of God stands forever. The comparison in Psalm 103:15 to 17 is the same, and Peter applies the Isaiah text to the gospel in 1 Peter 1:24-25. Human frailty is the backdrop against which God's endless love shines.

The father sees his son while he is still far off, 'was filled with compassion,' runs and embraces him. It is verse 13 as a story, and it also shows verse 12: the son's sin is not recounted but covered with a robe and a ring.

Jesus forgives the paralytic and then heals him. The scribes object that only God can forgive, which is precisely the point of Psalm 103:3. The healing is the visible sign of the invisible forgiveness the psalm puts first.

Mary sings 'His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation,' drawing on Psalm 103:17. The Magnificat places the coming of Jesus inside the long arc of mercy the psalm describes.

Explains how God can forgive without compromising justice, through the atoning sacrifice of Christ. It supplies the New Testament answer to the question hidden behind verse 10, how can He not repay us and yet remain just.
Our high priest can sympathize with our weaknesses. It deepens verse 14: the God who knows we are dust has also entered the dust Himself, and so knows human weakness from the inside.

Myriads of angels and every creature bless the One on the throne and the Lamb. It is the full realization of the call in Psalm 103:20 to 22 that angels, hosts and all God's works bless Him, now with the Lamb added to the praise.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a gift and a failure, and the opening chapters leave the reader asking whether God will deal with humanity as it deserves. Genesis 3:19 says 'dust you are, and to dust you shall return.' Psalm 103 is the answer which Israel received at the foot of Sinai and spent the rest of its history learning to say: He does not. 'He has not dealt with us according to our sins' (verse 10). What God said about Himself to Moses becomes a refrain in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms, so that every later generation of sinners can pray with confidence.

The psalm sits at a particular moment in that story, after the golden calf and before the exile. Israel had already shown they were dust, in the sense of verse 14: forgetful, stiff-necked, quick to turn. The psalm does not ignore it. It places forgiveness at the front of the list of benefits because it knows forgiveness is what the story needs most. Later the exile would test the claim, and the prophets would return to the same words, Joel 2:13 and Micah 7:18-19, to insist that God's mercy was still the last word.

The story's centre is the cross. The psalm asks how a holy God can remove sins as far as east from west without simply ignoring them, and the New Testament shows the answer: Christ bore them, Hebrews 9:26. The Gospels present Jesus as the one who does what the psalm says God does, forgives, heals and redeems, and who calls God 'Father' in a way that makes verse 13 a daily reality for His followers. The fear of the LORD, which the psalm mentions three times, becomes in the New Testament the reverent love of children.

The psalm also anticipates the end. Its last verses call every creature to bless the LORD, and Revelation 5:13 is the answer: 'every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea' praising the One on the throne and the Lamb. The grass that withers will give way to those whose life God has renewed, and the God whose loving devotion is 'from everlasting to everlasting' will have the last word. The soul that began alone, addressing itself, ends in a crowd, and every voice is saying what David first said: Bless the LORD.

sermon.title: Praying the Gospel
sermon.why: Preached directly on Psalm 103:1-22, as listed by Gospel in Life's own record of the sermon, Keller works through this psalm's call not to forget God's benefits, showing how remembering God's specific, gospel-shaped kindness transforms how believers pray and handle every circumstance of life.

quiz.q: What does David command his own soul to do in verses 1-2?

options.text: Bless the LORD and not forget all His kind deeds.
options.note: David deliberately addresses his own soul, commanding it to bless the LORD and actively remember His benefits.

options.text: Forget the past and focus only on the future.
options.note: David's command is the opposite, to deliberately remember, not forget, God's kind deeds.

options.text: Remain silent in reverent awe.
options.note: The psalm calls for active blessing and praise, not silence.

options.text: Wait for a new deliverance before offering any praise.
options.note: David commands his soul to bless the LORD now, based on remembered kindness, not waiting for a new deliverance first.

quiz.q: According to verses 3-5, what benefits does the LORD provide?

options.text: He forgives iniquities, heals diseases, redeems life from the Pit, crowns with loving devotion and compassion, and satisfies with good things.
options.note: These verses list five specific benefits: forgiveness, healing, redemption, crowning, and satisfaction.

options.text: Only material wealth and political power.
options.note: The named benefits are forgiveness, healing, redemption, love, and satisfaction, not wealth or political power.

options.text: Only protection from foreign armies.
options.note: Military protection is not named among these specific benefits.

options.text: Only the promise of a long earthly life with no mention of forgiveness.
options.note: Forgiveness of iniquities is explicitly named as the first benefit in verse 3, alongside healing, redemption, and compassion.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the removal of sin in verse 12?

options.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us.
options.note: This famous image conveys the completeness of God's removal of sin, since east and west never meet.

options.text: Sin is merely postponed until a future day of reckoning.
options.note: The psalm describes sin as actually removed, not merely postponed.

options.text: Sin is hidden but still present and unresolved.
options.note: The imagery conveys complete removal, not concealment of unresolved sin.

options.text: Sin is transferred to future generations to bear.
options.note: The psalm states sin is removed from us, not transferred forward to future generations.

quiz.q: What contrast does the psalm draw between human life and God's loving devotion in verses 15-17?

options.text: Human life is like grass that withers, but the LORD's loving devotion extends from everlasting to everlasting.
options.note: This is the psalm's central contrast between fleeting human life and God's eternal, steadfast love.

options.text: Human life and God's loving devotion are said to last exactly the same length of time.
options.note: The psalm draws a sharp contrast, not an equivalence, between brief human life and God's eternal love.

options.text: God's loving devotion is described as temporary and conditional on human performance.
options.note: The psalm describes God's loving devotion as everlasting, not temporary or performance-based.

options.text: Human life is described as permanent while God's love is fleeting.
options.note: The psalm reverses this: human life is fleeting like grass, while God's loving devotion is what endures forever.

quiz.q: Who is summoned to bless the LORD in the psalm's closing verses, 20-22?

options.text: God's mighty angels, all His hosts, and all His works in every place of His dominion.
options.note: The closing verses widen the call to bless the LORD to include angels, heavenly hosts, and the whole of creation.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the Jerusalem temple.
options.note: The call is far broader than the priesthood, extending to angels, hosts, and all creation.

options.text: Only the psalmist himself, with no wider audience.
options.note: While the psalm returns to 'Bless the LORD, O my soul' at the very end, verses 20-22 explicitly widen the call to angels, hosts, and all God's works.

options.text: Only the nations that had defeated Israel in battle.
options.note: The summons is cosmic in scope, to angels and all creation, not specifically to nations that had defeated Israel.

questions: David deliberately commands his own soul, 'Bless the LORD, O my soul,' rather than waiting for a feeling of gratitude to arise naturally. What specific kind deed of God might you need to deliberately name and remember today, even if you do not feel like praising Him?
The psalm lists concrete benefits, forgiveness, healing, redemption, compassion, satisfaction, rather than vague thanks. Which of these benefits do you most need to remember and rest in right now?

'As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us.' What specific sin or guilt are you still carrying that this psalm invites you to release, trusting it has truly been removed in Christ?
The psalm contrasts fleeting human life, like grass, with God's everlasting loving devotion. How does remembering the brevity of your own days change what you prioritize this week?

The psalm ends by summoning angels, heavenly hosts, and all creation to bless the LORD alongside one solitary soul. How does it change your sense of worship to know that your own praise joins a chorus far larger than yourself?

translationNotes.note: The image of youth 'renewed like the eagle's' likely draws on the ancient perception of the eagle as a symbol of vigor and longevity, picturing restored strength rather than literal transformation into a bird.

This verse closely echoes God's own self-description to Moses in Exodus 34:6, 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,' a foundational Old Testament summary of God's character quoted or echoed throughout the rest of Scripture.

'He knows our frame' uses a Hebrew word related to the verb for forming or shaping used in Genesis 2:7, where God forms man from the dust, tying this psalm's language of compassion directly back to creation itself.
